Potassium-sparing diuretics: 2

A patient receives amiloride, which acts directly on sodium entry in the collecting system without blocking the aldosterone receptor. Which transport mechanism distinguishes this potassium-sparing diuretic from spironolactone in the same broad class?

  1. NCC inhibition in the distal convoluted tubule
  2. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism
  3. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition
  4. ENaC blockade in the collecting system
  5. NKCC2 inhibition in the thick ascending limb
Answer and explanation

ENaC blockade in the collecting system

Amiloride and triamterene directly block epithelial sodium channels.

Option explanations

ENaC blockade in the collecting system: Amiloride and triamterene directly block epithelial sodium channels.

NKCC2 inhibition in the thick ascending limb: Loop diuretics inhibit sodium-potassium-chloride transport in the thick ascending limb. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

NCC inhibition in the distal convoluted tubule: Thiazides inhibit the distal sodium-chloride cotransporter. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism: Spironolactone and eplerenone block aldosterone signaling and reduce potassium secretion. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibition: Acetazolamide reduces bicarbonate reabsorption, predominantly in the proximal tubule. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
